paras: The ordered whipping of Rev. Thomas Collins took place in Yazoo, Mississippi, in about March 1919, when the town's white Commercial Club ordered the Black minister and four other colored citizens beaten for defying a ban on Black newspapers. Collins escaped on the way to the whipping post and fled to Philadelphia, and the Baltimore Afro-American presented his case as an example of a "Ku Klux Law Against Reading Colored Newspapers and Magazines."

According to Collins's account, white people in Yazoo had ordered that no race literature be circulated in the town. Collins read colored newspapers despite the order, and he also advised his congregation not to attend a lecturer who announced that "colored people ought to stay in the South with their only friends."

White ministers called Collins up and questioned him, and he was then taken before the white Commercial Club, where his pockets were searched for letters and papers. The club ordered him taken out and beaten together with four other colored citizens, whose names were not reported. On the way to the whipping post Collins got away, though the printed text describing his escape is garbled.

He then traveled to Jackson, a distance the headline gave as 46 miles and the story as fifty, and took a train to Philadelphia. Several other people from his town were with him, among them an agent of the Crisis.
In Philadelphia Collins reported to Bishop Levine why he had left his charge. No report of an arrest or of the fate of the four others appears in the coverage.

Only the Baltimore Afro-American is known to have carried the story, on its front page of April 4, 1919, under a Philadelphia dateline and the headline "MINISTER FLEES MISSISSIPPI CITY." Its deck attributed the ban to the "Ku Klux."

A week later an Afro-American editorial answering the Belzoni Banner's claims about Mississippi said that a Yazoo minister had "faced a whipping post because he read colored newspapers and magazines" and "fled to the North for his life." The editorial grouped the case with the expulsion of Booker T. Washington Jr. from Alabama and the lynching of a soldier in Georgia as "bits of every day news from Southern states."

reader.title: Ordered whipping of Rev. Thomas Collins
bases: A3 reports that a white Commercial Club ordered Collins and four other colored citizens taken out and beaten at a whipping post for defying a ban on race literature, and the headline calls the ban a "Ku Klux Law"; Collins escaped before any beating, so the act reported against him is an ordered, not completed, whipping.

Only the Baltimore Afro-American reported the case: a Philadelphia-datelined front-page story (A3) and a one-sentence editorial reference a week later in the same paper (A4), both resting on Collins's own account; no other paper's report was found.

accounts.label: Collins's account via the Afro-American
accounts.gist: Collins said white ministers questioned him and the white Commercial Club ordered him and four others beaten for reading race papers and counseling his congregation against a stay-in-the-South lecturer; he escaped on the way to the whipping post and fled north.

accounts.label: Afro-American editorial
accounts.gist: A week later the paper's editorial said a Yazoo minister had faced a whipping post for reading colored newspapers and magazines and fled North for his life.

framing.detail: Front-page headline 'MINISTER FLEES MISSISSIPPI CITY' with a deck calling the ban a 'Ku Klux Law Against Reading Colored Newspapers and Magazines'; the editorial listed the case among 'bits of every day news from Southern states' rebutting claims that law-abiding colored people are never disturbed.

conflicts.note: Both figures appear in the same article; the body text around the escape is garbled, so the manner of escape is not legible.

record_check.dossier: A whipping was ordered but Collins escaped before it; no beating of him is reported, and no order to leave is reported (he fled on his own after escaping). Better: threat (ordered whipping), seizure/search; flight.
